record.title: Zero-field zero-candidate descent
record.locator: Theorem 6 and its proof, printed pp.13–16, especially equation (24): zero-coefficient heat response and a feasible late-step improvement. The exposition separately derives the origin-atom directional derivative.

aligned_passages.text:
\Needspace{11\baselineskip}

### 7.1 Why the zero candidate does not minimise

Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,
the state is $B_t$. Differentiating the slope once more gives

$$
X_t=B_t,\qquad
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi(1-t)}}e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}.
$$

A Gaussian integral gives
$\mathbb E e^{-B_t^2/(1-t)}=\sqrt{(1-t)/(1+t)}$. Substituting
into $q_0'=\mathbb E[a_0(t,B_t)^2]$ and integrating from zero yields

$$
q_0'(t)=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

This recovers the half-time value $1/3$. It also shows that
$q_0(t)\to1$ while $q_0'(t)\to\infty$: convergence of a function
at one does not bound its derivative there.
The constant direction $\eta=1$ is admissible and adds an atom at zero.
Its cost is

$$
D\mathcal P(0)[1]
=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
=\frac14-\frac1\pi<0.
$$

So a small positive constant coefficient improves the zero candidate.
This calculation uses the heat and variation formulas, not a minimiser
hypothesis; see also [Chen–Handschy–Lerman, proof of Theorem 6][chl-optimality].

### 7.4 Answers to the questions **[Question 1](#question-1).** Adding mass at $1/2$ gives cumulative heights $0,2,2+\varepsilon,3+\varepsilon$, in their successive intervals; removing it at $1/4$ gives heights $0,2-\varepsilon,3-\varepsilon$. Both functions remain nonnegative and nondecreasing. Removing mass at $1/2$ instead lowers the height from $2$ to $2-\varepsilon$ there, creating a downward jump, so it is forbidden even though all values remain nonnegative. Scaling both weights preserves all admissibility conditions. These tests concern allowed candidates; a smaller ordinary area alone does not establish a smaller Parisi value. **[Question 2](#question-2).** For $\gamma=0$, the state is $X_{1/4}=B_{1/4}$, a centred Gaussian with variance $1/4$, so it has the law of $Z/2$. The remaining independent Gaussian noise $B_1-B_{1/4}$ has variance $3/4$ and standard deviation $\sqrt3/2$. Thus $$ q_0(1/4)=\int_{\mathbb R} \left(2F_{\mathrm G}(z/\sqrt3)-1\right)^2\varphi(z)\,dz. $$ The two variances agree at half time, but not here. For nonzero $z$, the magnitude of the response is now smaller, so $q_0(1/4)<1/3$. The arcsine formula in Section 7.1 also gives this comparison. Changing the coefficient after $1/2$ leaves $X_{1/4}=B_{1/4}$: its drift has been zero up to that time. The remaining Brownian noise still has variance $3/4$, but the value now includes future control terms. Its slope must be recomputed before averaging the square against the unchanged state law. Thus the displayed integral using $u_0$ is no longer justified. Knowing the future coefficient schedule does not reveal future random noise. **[Question 3](#question-3).** A strictly convex $f'$ lies below its endpoint chord. That chord has mean height $(1/2+3/2)/2=1$, hence integral three. Therefore $f(5)-f(2)=\int_2^5f'(t)\,dt<3$, contradicting the prescribed values. With non-strict convexity the data are possible: $f(t)=2+(t-2)/2+(t-2)^2/6$ has affine derivative and satisfies all four endpoint values. The argument needs a strict loss of area; the common endpoint upper bound of one in Figure 2 is convenient, not essential. This is a calculus example, not a candidate SK moment function. With the right slope changed to $2$, the chord has mean $5/4$, so a strict loss of area can leave the required mean one. Indeed, $$ f(t)=2+\frac{t-2}{2}+\frac{(t-2)^3}{18} $$ has the required endpoint values, slopes $1/2$ and $2$, and $(f')''=1/3>0$. Thus these changed data are compatible. Strict convexity produces the contradiction only when the chord cannot supply enough area. **[Question 4](#question-4).** Set $h=q'-1$. Since $q(r)=r$, reaching or passing the diagonal at $t$ means $\int_r^t h\ge0$. Strict convexity places $h$ below its endpoint chord, so that integral is less than $(t-r)(h(r)+h(t))/2$. With $h(r)\le0$, this forces $h(t)>0$. The chord rule on $[r,s]$, solved for $h(s)$, keeps every later value at least $h(t)$. Integrating gives $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))>1$ for a suitable $s<1$, violating the bound. If $q$ never reaches the diagonal, then $G(r)<0$ instead. Thus both possibilities contradict the conditions on a minimiser. For the proposed polynomial, $q(0)=0$, $q'(0)=1$, $q'''=6>0$, and direct integration gives $G(s)=s^3(1-s)/4\ge0$, with $G(0)=0$. Its derivative has minimum $13/16$, so $q$ increases to $5/4$ as $t\uparrow1$. It is bounded, but $q(9/10)=2043/2000>1$. The other reduced conditions therefore do not replace the exact cap supplied by $|u|\le1$. **[Question 5](#question-5).** Choose $r=0.4$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. The theorem gives a pair differing on between 29% and 31% of sites. Reverse every sign of the second configuration. Its energy is unchanged, its overlap changes sign, and the differing-site fraction becomes its complement, between 69% and 71%. This operation uses the same successful instance and causes no further probability loss. The theorem fixes $\eta>0$ before $n$ grows; it supplies no rate justifying $\eta=1/n$. This stronger choice is not established by the stated result.
